title: The Shadow of the Living Light
subtitle: Hildegard of Bingen's visions made public, Disibodenberg, Trier and the Rupertsberg, 1141–1153, with a coda to 1175
intro: In 1141 a forty-two-year-old nun in a monastery on the Nahe saw, by her own later account, a fiery light pour into her mind and heard a command to write. For a decade she wrote, slowly and privately, with one monk and one young nun as witnesses. Then she did something unusual for a visionary: before letting the book go out, she sent it upward, first in a letter to Bernard of Clairvaux, then through her abbot and the archbishop of Mainz, until, by her biographers' account, Pope Eugenius III read from it aloud at a synod in Trier in the winter of 1147–48.

This chapter's record is not a diary. It is a preface written into the book itself, a run of dated letters, a memoir Hildegard dictated in old age that survives inside her saint's life, and that saint's life itself, the Vita, begun by Gottfried around 1174 and finished by Theoderich of Echternach after her death. Each entry is labelled for what it is. The most famous scene, the pope reading Scivias at Trier, is known only from the Vita, and papal letters to her come down through collections that were revised and rearranged after she died, above all the great Riesenkodex in Wiesbaden.

Around Hildegard stand the people who checked, used, doubted or lost something to the new prophet: Bernard's cautious reply; Abbot Kuno, who passed her writings upward and then tried to stop her leaving; a Paris master and a neighbouring abbess who wrote with questions within months of Trier; Richardis von Stade, the nun who helped write the book and then left to be an abbess, and her brother Archbishop Hartwig, who wrote the letter reporting her death; and Elisabeth of Schönau, a younger visionary who came to Hildegard after her own public prophecies had failed.

There are gaps. Richardis left no words that survive, and her wishes reach us only through people who wanted her back or wanted her gone. Kuno's side of the move is told by Hildegard's biographers. Volmar, the scribe, appears in his own voice only in one late letter whose companion reply is questioned. The illuminated Rupertsberg Scivias, whose pictures are reproduced everywhere, vanished from Dresden in 1945.

A coda jumps to 1175, when a monk of Gembloux, Guibert, asked her directly how she saw. Her answer, that the light came while she was awake and never in sleep, dream or madness, is the fullest firsthand description of the experience. In 1913 and 1917 the physician-historian Charles Singer read those words and the manuscript pictures as signs of migraine aura. That reading appears here as a modern position, not a verdict, alongside her own.
calendar_note: All medieval dates are in the Julian calendar, which was in use throughout; date_iso gives them as historians cite them (proleptic Julian), with no conversion. Hildegard dated the 1141 vision by the year of the Incarnation and by her own age, 42 years and 7 months, which implies a birth in 1098. Most letters carry no day or month and are dated by editors to a range of years; those ranges are shown as given in the Van Acker edition and the Baird–Ehrman translation. Only Richardis's death (29 October 1152) and Hildegard's death (17 September 1179) are known to the day.
seam: These records show a private experience held back for years, written down with only two witnesses, and then deliberately checked against the highest authorities before it went public. Approval did not end the testing: questions, rival claims and personal costs followed. A reality that begins inside one mind becomes shared through letters, signatures and a pope's reading, and eight centuries later it is reread through a new shared framework, neurology. As in Le Guin's The Lathe of Heaven, the question is who gets to decide what a vision has changed.

eyes.name: Hildegard of Bingen
eyes.role: Benedictine magistra of the women's community at Disibodenberg (elected 1136), aged 42 in 1141; from c. 1150 head of her own house on the Rupertsberg near Bingen
eyes.where: Disibodenberg on the Nahe, then the Rupertsberg opposite Bingen
eyes.form: preface to a visionary book, dated letters, and a dictated memoir preserved in her Vita
eyes.authenticity: Scivias (1141–51) survives in the Wiesbaden Riesenkodex (Hs. 2, c. 1180s) and other copies; the illuminated Rupertsberg Scivias was lost from Dresden in 1945 and is known from a 1920s hand-painted facsimile and microfilm. Her letters (ed. Van Acker and Klaes-Hachmöller, CCCM 91–91B) survive in several collections; the late Riesenkodex versions were stylistically revised, probably partly by Guibert of Gembloux, and some pairings of letter and reply there cannot be trusted. The first-person memoir passages in Book II of the Vita are her own words as quoted by Theoderich.
eyes.bio: A noble-born oblate enclosed at Disibodenberg as a girl, she said she had seen a strange light since early childhood but kept it almost wholly to herself until 1141. Her angle is unique because she both had the experience and controlled how it was written down, defended and finally described to a curious outsider thirty-four years later.

sources.title: Letter to Bernard, CCCM 91 ep. 1, Epistolae
Baird & Ehrman, The Letters of Hildegard of Bingen, vol. 1 (PDF)

eyes.name: Volmar of Disibodenberg
eyes.role: Monk of Disibodenberg, Hildegard's teacher, confessor and scribe; later provost of the Rupertsberg. Almost nothing in his own hand survives from 1141–53; he is seen mainly through Hildegard's Scivias preface and the Vita.
eyes.form: one late letter (c. 1170–73); otherwise known through others
eyes.authenticity: His letter to Hildegard survives with a long 'reply' in the Riesenkodex as the so-called Testamentum propheticum; Van Acker printed Volmar's letter in full but the reply only in part, and scholars (e.g. John Van Engen, 2018) question whether the two form a genuine exchange.
eyes.bio: The unnamed 'faithful man' of the Scivias preface, the only person besides Jutta to whom Hildegard first confided the visions. He took down and corrected her Latin for some thirty years, and his anxious late letter asks who will answer the community's questions once she is gone.

sources.title: Van Engen, review of Narvaja ed., Testamentum propheticum (sehepunkte 2018)

eyes.name: Kuno, Abbot of Disibodenberg
eyes.role: Abbot of the double monastery of Disibodenberg, Hildegard's superior in 1141–50. No surviving firsthand account of the visions or the move from him found beyond a short late letter; his actions are known from Hildegard's letters and the Vita.
eyes.vantage_label: the superior who first passed the writings upward
eyes.form: known through others; one letter attributed to him
eyes.authenticity: The Vita (secondhand) credits him with reporting her writings to Archbishop Heinrich of Mainz and with resisting, then allowing, the move to the Rupertsberg. A letter from Kuno asking her for revelations about St Disibod is preserved in her correspondence; its exact date (before his death in 1155) is not secure.
eyes.bio: He stood to lose a famous nun, her noble sisters and their endowments when she left, and the Vita remembers him as the man who first resisted her. He is a useful reminder that 'checking with authority' began at home, with an abbot who had his own interests.

eyes.name: Bernard of Clairvaux
eyes.role: Cistercian abbot of Clairvaux, the most influential churchman in Latin Europe, then preaching the Second Crusade (1146–47)
eyes.where: Clairvaux, Champagne; at Trier with the pope in winter 1147–48 (per the Vita)
eyes.authenticity: His short reply is Bernard ep. 366 in the Leclercq–Rochais Opera (vol. 7) and also ep. 1r in Hildegard's Epistolarium; it is accepted as genuine. His role at Trier rests on the Vita.
eyes.bio: Hildegard chose him as her first outside judge. His reply is brief and cautious, yet his name lent her a protection no abbot could.

eyes.name: Pope Eugenius III (Bernardo of Pisa)
eyes.role: Pope from 1145, a former Cistercian monk under Bernard; in the Rhineland in 1147–48 and presiding over the synod at Trier
eyes.vantage_label: the highest judge, reading her book aloud
eyes.authenticity: The famous scene of Eugenius reading Scivias at Trier comes only from the Vita, written decades later after his death and largely after hers (secondhand). Papal letters to Hildegard survive mainly in her own letter collections, including the Riesenkodex, whose versions were revised and rearranged to present her as a prophet; the letters in his name are therefore treated here with caution and their exact wording is not relied on.
eyes.bio: A pope who had been Bernard's monk, he gave the authorisation that turned a private manuscript into a public prophecy. Yet his own voice in the record is faint and filtered through her archive.

sources.title: Van Engen on the Riesenkodex arrangement (sehepunkte 2018)

eyes.name: Gottfried of Disibodenberg
eyes.role: Monk of Disibodenberg who became Hildegard's secretary in 1174 and began her Vita (Book I) while she was still alive
eyes.authenticity: Book I of the Vita sanctae Hildegardis, written c. 1174–76 from the community's memory and documents; it is the main source for the Trier synod and the papal approval. Secondhand for all events of 1141–53.
eyes.bio: He was not at Trier and not at Disibodenberg in the 1140s as a witness of record; he wrote at Rupertsberg with Hildegard in her seventies. His account is the official story her community wanted told.

eyes.name: Theoderich of Echternach
eyes.role: Monk of Echternach commissioned after Hildegard's death to complete her Vita
eyes.vantage_label: posthumous editor of her own memoir
eyes.form: hagiographical life incorporating her dictated memoir
eyes.authenticity: Books II–III of the Vita, completed in the 1180s; Theoderich quotes long first-person passages that he says Hildegard dictated (labelled 'later firsthand' here), alongside miracles and his own framing (secondhand).
eyes.bio: He never met her as far as the record shows. His value is that he kept her own words about the 1140s, including the illness and the move, inside a saint's life.

sources.title: Riesenkodex, which contains the Vita (HLB Wiesbaden)

eyes.name: Odo of Soissons (Odo of Paris)
eyes.role: Master in the Paris schools, later abbot of Ourscamp
eyes.authenticity: His letter to Hildegard (dated 1148 by Baird & Ehrman / Atherton) and her reply (1148–50) survive in her collection.
eyes.bio: Within months of Trier the news had reached Paris. Odo's letter shows the professional theologians probing whether her gift could settle a disputed school question.

eyes.name: Tengswich of Andernach
eyes.role: Magistra (superior) of the canonesses at Andernach on the Rhine
eyes.authenticity: Letter 52 in Baird & Ehrman (1148–50) with Hildegard's reply 52r; a later 'cleaned-up' revision of the exchange (Letters 53/53r) also exists, showing how the collection was edited.
eyes.bio: Polite on the surface and pointed underneath, she asks why Hildegard's nuns wear silk veils, crowns and unbound hair and why only noble women are admitted. Hers is the clearest contemporary voice of doubt.

eyes.name: Richardis von Stade
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found. Noble nun of Hildegard's community, her helper in writing Scivias and a beloved companion; elected abbess of Bassum in 1151, she died there on 29 October 1152. Her own letters, if she wrote any, are lost; she is known only through Hildegard's letters and her brother's.
eyes.where: Disibodenberg and Rupertsberg, then Bassum near Bremen
eyes.vantage_label: the silent witness who helped write the book
eyes.form: no surviving record of her own
eyes.authenticity: Her part in Scivias rests on Hildegard's preface ('a noble girl' bore witness) and the Vita; her death date on Hartwig's letter.
eyes.bio: She shared the decade of writing and then left for an abbacy her family secured. Her silence is the chapter's largest gap: everything about her wishes comes through people who wanted her back or wanted her gone.

eyes.name: Hartwig of Stade, Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen
eyes.role: Richardis's brother; archbishop of Bremen from 1148, in whose diocese Bassum lay
eyes.vantage_label: the brother who took her away
eyes.authenticity: His letter reporting Richardis's death (Letter 13, 1152) and Hildegard's reply (13r) are in her collection.
eyes.bio: He backed his sister's election, received Hildegard's furious appeal, and then wrote the letter that ended the dispute. His admission of fault is rare in the whole archive.

sources.title: Letter to Hartwig (October 1152), Fordham Medieval Hollywood

eyes.name: Elisabeth of Schönau
eyes.role: Benedictine nun at Schönau in the Taunus, a visionary from 1152; later magistra
eyes.vantage_label: the younger visionary seeking a precedent
eyes.authenticity: Her letters to Hildegard survive in her own collection (ed. Roth 1884; trans. Anne L. Clark 2000) and Hildegard's reply is CCCM 91A ep. 201r. Her works were edited and promoted by her brother Ekbert.
eyes.bio: Two decades younger and visited by an angel rather than a light, she was mocked when a forecast of disaster attributed to her did not come true. She wrote to Hildegard as the one person who had already passed through public testing.

eyes.name: Guibert of Gembloux
eyes.role: Monk of Gembloux in Brabant; correspondent from 1175, Hildegard's secretary at the Rupertsberg from 1177
eyes.vantage_label: curious outsider who became an insider
eyes.authenticity: His letters survive in his own collection (CCCM 66–66A); Hildegard's reply on her way of seeing is in her Epistolarium. He is also thought to have polished the late versions of her letters.
eyes.bio: He asked the questions a careful reader would ask: did she dream, fall into ecstasy, forget? Her answer to him, at about seventy-seven, is the fullest firsthand description of how the visions felt.

sources.title: Newman, 'Hildegard of Bingen: Visions and Validation', Church History 1985

eyes.name: Charles Singer
eyes.role: British physician and historian of science and medicine, aged 37 when he first presented his reading in 1913
eyes.authenticity: 'The Scientific Views and Visions of Saint Hildegard', in Studies in the History and Method of Science (Oxford, 1917), building on a November 1913 lecture. A medical interpretation, given here as one position among others.
eyes.bio: Studying the Wiesbaden and Rupertsberg manuscripts and their pictures of stars, fire and spreading light, he proposed that the visions matched migraine aura. Katherine Foxhall (2014) traces how his retrospective diagnosis later hardened into received 'fact'.

sources.title: Foxhall, 'Making Modern Migraine Medieval', Medical History 2014

entries.headline: Jutta dies and Hildegard becomes magistra
entries.digest: Jutta of Sponheim, the anchoress who had raised her, died, and the enclosed women elected Hildegard to lead them. In the Scivias preface Jutta is remembered as one of only two people who had known about the visions before 1141. Hildegard was now responsible for a small community inside a men's monastery.
entries.source_note: Election as magistra from the Vita (Atherton chronology); Jutta as the noble woman who knew of the visions per the Scivias Protestificatio.

entries.headline: A fiery light floods her mind: write what you see
entries.digest: In the preface to Scivias she dates the decisive experience to the 1141st year of the Incarnation, when she was forty-two years and seven months old. A fiery light of great brightness came from the opened heavens, poured through her whole brain and warmed rather than burned her heart and breast, and suddenly she understood the meaning of scripture. A voice ordered her to speak and write what she saw and heard.
entries.quote: cum quadraginta duorum annorum septemque mensium essem
entries.source_note: Scivias, Protestificatio (Latin, CCCM 43); Latin text cited in Fraboschi, Stylos 15 (2006). The preface itself was written during or at the end of the ten-year composition, not on the day.

entries.headline: Refusing to write until illness forces her
entries.digest: The same preface admits that she had seen this power and light since girlhood but told almost no one. Even after the command she held back out of doubt and fear of what people would say, until a long illness pressed her to begin. Then, with the witness of a noble girl and of the monk she trusted, she set her hand to writing.
entries.source_note: Scivias, Protestificatio; the 'monk' is identified with Volmar and the 'girl' with Richardis by the Vita and later scholars.

entries.headline: The faithful monk becomes the scribe
entries.digest: Hildegard's preface describes the man she sought out and found faithful, who took down her words. Volmar left no account of these sessions himself; what is known is her description and the later frontispiece of the Rupertsberg Scivias, which shows a monk at a window beside her as she writes on wax tablets.
entries.form: described in Hildegard's preface; later illumination
entries.source_note: Scivias Protestificatio; Christian History Institute profile; Rupertsberg Scivias frontispiece (c. 1165–80, known from facsimile).

entries.headline: An anxious letter to Bernard of Clairvaux
entries.digest: She wrote to the great abbot that she was troubled by a vision received in the spirit, which she had kept secret except from one monk. She called herself untaught in letters, explained that her understanding came inwardly, and asked whether she should speak openly or stay silent. She added that she had seen Bernard himself in a vision more than two years earlier.
entries.source_note: Hildegard ep. 1 (CCCM 91), trans. Baird & Ehrman; https://epistolae.ctl.columbia.edu/letter/1188.html

entries.headline: Bernard's short, careful reply
entries.digest: Bernard answered more briefly than, he said, he would have liked. He put her praise of him down to her humility, rejoiced at the grace of God in her, and urged her to respond to it with humility and devotion. He asked what he could teach someone already taught inwardly, and requested her prayers.
entries.source_note: Bernard ep. 366 (Leclercq–Rochais vol. 7) = Hildegard ep. 1r; https://epistolae.ctl.columbia.edu/letter/1189.html

entries.headline: The abbot carries her writings to Mainz
entries.digest: According to the Vita, Volmar informed Abbot Kuno, who after consulting his monks reported the matter to Archbishop Heinrich of Mainz. From Mainz the matter was brought to the pope. This chain of reporting is the Vita's version, written about a generation later.
entries.source_note: Vita sanctae Hildegardis I; summarised in Baird & Ehrman, introduction.

entries.headline: Papal envoys sent to fetch the book
entries.digest: The Vita says that Pope Eugenius, staying at Trier for a synod, sent trusted clergy to Disibodenberg to inquire quietly and bring back part of what she had written. The envoys returned with the unfinished Scivias. No document from the envoys themselves survives.
entries.source_note: Vita I; synod dates from standard chronologies (Eugenius at Trier winter 1147–48). The names of the envoys are not relied on here.

entries.headline: The pope reads Scivias aloud to the synod
entries.digest: In the Vita's telling, Eugenius himself read from her writings before the archbishop, cardinals and clergy gathered at Trier, and Bernard spoke in support. The pope then wrote to her, allowing and urging her to continue writing. This is the scene that made her famous, and it is known only from her biographers.
entries.source_note: Vita I; Baird & Ehrman intro; Hildegard Society FAQ ('according to her Uita').

entries.headline: A papal letter preserved in her own archive
entries.digest: Letters in Eugenius's name appear in Hildegard's collections, encouraging her and later dealing with Rupertsberg and Richardis business. Because the surviving texts come through collections that were revised and ordered by rank after her death, how much is the pope's own wording is uncertain. They show at least that her community treated papal contact as the seal on her authority.
entries.source_note: Baird & Ehrman, introduction (Riesenkodex 'highly unreliable'); Van Engen 2018 on the Riesenkodex arrangement. Authenticity of the exact wording not established.

entries.date_display: shortly after the Synod of Trier (1148)
entries.headline: Writing to the pope who approved her
entries.digest: Atherton places her letter to Eugenius shortly after the synod. In it she speaks in the voice of the light that taught her and presses the pope to keep the writings alive and give them his support, rather than letting them be lost.
entries.source_note: Hildegard to Eugenius III, trans. in Atherton, Selected Writings; date range per Atherton.

entries.headline: A Paris master hears of the new prophet
entries.digest: Odo wrote that word had reached him of her visions and that she was said to produce new songs without having studied music. He asked her to settle a theological question then debated in the schools, about whether God's paternity and divinity are themselves God. Within a year of Trier her reputation had crossed into the Paris schools.
entries.source_note: Odo to Hildegard, dated 1148 in Atherton (trans.) and Baird & Ehrman.

entries.headline: Answering Odo from the living light
entries.digest: Her reply refused the schoolmen's terms. Rather than argue as a master, she answered from what she said she saw, insisting on God's simple fullness, and spoke as one taught by the light rather than by books.
entries.source_note: Hildegard to Odo (1148–50), trans. Atherton.

entries.headline: Silk veils and noble girls: a neighbour's doubts
entries.digest: Tengswich wrote that strange reports had reached her: on feast days Hildegard's nuns stood in church with unbound hair, white silk veils, gold crowns and rings, and the community admitted only women of noble birth. Under courteous greetings she asked how this squared with scripture and the apostles' poverty.
entries.source_note: Tengswich to Hildegard, Letter 52, Baird & Ehrman vol. 1 (1148–50).

entries.headline: Defending virgins in festival dress
entries.digest: Hildegard replied that the rules on modest dress for married women did not bind consecrated virgins, who stood in the unfading greenness of paradise and could wear white and crowns as brides. On admitting only nobles, she argued that ranks should not be mixed in one fold. The exchange was later rewritten into a smoother version.
entries.source_note: Hildegard ep. 52r; revised version Letters 53/53r noted by Baird & Ehrman.

entries.headline: Shown a new place, she falls ill when refused
entries.digest: In passages Theoderich says she dictated, Hildegard recalled being shown in the light the place where she should move with her sisters, the Rupertsberg above the Nahe at Bingen. When the abbot and monks opposed it, she lay sick and could not be moved until the permission came.
entries.source_note: Vita II (autobiographical passages); Christian History Institute; Atherton chronology.

entries.headline: Kuno yields after seeing her stricken
entries.digest: The Vita presents the abbot's consent as a sign: Kuno, having seen her helpless, recognised that he was resisting God and let the women go. Theoderich wrote this after both Kuno and Hildegard were dead.
entries.source_note: Vita II; Christian History Institute (Kuno delayed the move until her illness).

entries.headline: About twenty nuns move to a bare hill
entries.digest: She remembered the move as costly. The new house was poor and unfinished, some sisters who had left wealthier conditions complained or went away, and people said the move was her own wilful idea. She described this hardship as a test that followed the permission.
entries.source_note: Vita II; Rupertsberg foundation 1150 (Hildegard Society FAQ).

entries.headline: Scivias finished after ten years
entries.digest: The preface says she worked on the book for ten years. The completed Scivias (Know the Ways) set out twenty-six visions with their explanations. The illuminated copy that later carried the famous pictures was made in the Rupertsberg scriptorium decades afterwards.
entries.source_note: Scivias, Protestificatio (ten years); completion 1151 in Atherton chronology and Fraboschi (1141–1151).

entries.headline: A furious letter to Richardis's mother
entries.digest: When Richardis was elected abbess of Bassum, Hildegard wrote to the Marchioness of Stade begging her not to take her daughter and calling the office a worldly honour obtained against God's will. Baird & Ehrman class this letter as particularly vehement.
entries.source_note: Hildegard to Marchioness Richardis von Stade; noted in Baird & Ehrman intro (not in vol. 1). Exact month not known.

entries.headline: Refusing the archbishop of Mainz
entries.digest: Archbishop Heinrich of Mainz ordered her to release Richardis to her new post. Hildegard refused and sent back a reply in the voice of the light, condemning the election as bought rather than God-given.
entries.source_note: Heinrich to Hildegard, Letter 18, and her reply 18r, Baird & Ehrman vol. 1.

entries.headline: The pope passes the dispute back to Mainz
entries.digest: Hildegard appealed to Eugenius; her letter is lost. In the papal letter preserved in her collection, the pope refers the matter of Richardis to Archbishop Heinrich of Mainz rather than ruling on it himself.
entries.source_note: Baird & Ehrman Letter 4 and headnote to Letter 12. Same caution on wording as above.

entries.headline: A lament addressed to Richardis herself
entries.digest: Writing directly to Richardis, Hildegard poured out grief: she had loved her nobility of character and wisdom, and felt abandoned. She warned that trusting in high birth and worldly honour was dangerous. No answer from Richardis survives.
entries.source_note: Hildegard to Richardis, Letter 64, Baird & Ehrman.

entries.headline: Appeal to the brother archbishop
entries.digest: She asked Hartwig of Bremen, in whose diocese Bassum lay, to send his sister back. She charged that the election was tainted by simony and blamed Abbot Kuno for interfering. It was one of her last moves in a dispute she was losing.
entries.source_note: Hildegard to Hartwig, Letter 12 (1151–52), Baird & Ehrman with headnote.

entries.headline: Richardis dies at Bassum
entries.digest: Richardis died suddenly at Bassum. The date is known from her brother's letter, which is the only record of her last days.
entries.source_note: Hartwig to Hildegard, Letter 13 (1152), Baird & Ehrman.

entries.headline: A brother admits he was wrong
entries.digest: Hartwig wrote to tell Hildegard that his sister had died. He said that before her death she had longed for Hildegard's cloister and would have returned, and he admitted that the fault in the dispute lay with him. He asked Hildegard to love Richardis as much as Richardis had loved her.
entries.source_note: Letter 13, Baird & Ehrman; Fordham item 'Letter to Hartwig (October 1152)'.

entries.headline: Forgiving, and turning grief into praise
entries.digest: Hildegard answered with forgiveness. She praised Richardis's virtue, set aside her bitterness at Hartwig's actions, and echoed her own sacred drama, the Ordo Virtutum, in describing a soul that had loved God.
entries.source_note: Hildegard to Hartwig, Letter 13r (1152), Baird & Ehrman notes 1–2.

entries.headline: The abbot asks the visionary about his saint
entries.digest: A letter in Kuno's name asks Hildegard to tell what God might reveal to her about St Disibod, the founder of his monastery. The man who had resisted her move now sought her gift for his own house.
entries.source_note: Kuno to Hildegard in her Epistolarium; Kuno died 1155 (Christian History Institute). Exact date not secure.

entries.date_display: 4 December 1154 (feast of St Barbara) to Easter 1155
entries.headline: An angel's warning and a forecast that failed
entries.digest: Elisabeth later recounted that from the feast of St Barbara her angel repeatedly ordered her to announce God's warnings. After resisting she gave her abbot a small book of visions; he preached them, letters with dire threats circulated in his name without his knowledge, and when the predicted punishment did not come at Easter, she was mocked.
entries.source_note: Elisabeth to Hildegard, ed. Roth 1884 Bk 3 ch. 19; trans. Clark 2000; https://epistolae.ctl.columbia.edu/letter/123.html

entries.headline: Asking Hildegard for consolation
entries.digest: Elisabeth wrote that gossip and mockery from religious people were hurting her, denied that she had ever predicted the Day of Judgment, and asked Hildegard for prayers and a reply. She wrote to the older woman as someone who had already faced testing and come through.
entries.source_note: Elisabeth to Hildegard (letter undated; written after Easter 1155); https://epistolae.ctl.columbia.edu/letter/123.html

entries.headline: The trumpet that sounds only when blown
entries.digest: Hildegard replied from her own fear and suffering. Human beings are clay vessels; those who speak God's mysteries are like a trumpet that sounds only when someone else breathes into it, so they must never take the sound for their own. She warned Elisabeth that pride tempts the inspired and called herself a faint, fearful trumpet.
entries.source_note: Hildegard ep. 201r, CCCM 91A pp. 456–57; https://epistolae.ctl.columbia.edu/letter/125.html

entries.headline: Who will answer us when you are gone?
entries.digest: In his late letter Volmar wrote in grief at the thought of her death: who would then answer the community's questions, who would reveal new things, and who would explain the scriptures? The letter survives with a long reply attributed to Hildegard, whose genuineness as a real reply is questioned.
entries.source_note: Volmar to Hildegard (Riesenkodex); Narvaja ed. 2014; Van Engen review 2018. Volmar d. 1173.

entries.headline: Gottfried begins the official life
entries.digest: Gottfried came from Disibodenberg as her secretary in 1174 and began the Vita, gathering the story of her childhood, the 1141 command, the papal approval and the move. He died in 1176 with the work unfinished.
entries.source_note: Atherton chronology (1174 arrival); Hildegard Society FAQ (Gottfried d. 1176).

entries.headline: A Flemish monk's questions
entries.digest: Guibert wrote with a mixture of curiosity and awe, comparing her to Deborah and Judith while warning her to stay humble. He asked practical questions: did she receive the visions in dreams or in ecstasy, did she dictate in Latin or in German, and did she forget what she saw?
entries.source_note: Newman 1985 (quoting Guibert's 1175 letter); Atherton chronology.

entries.headline: How she sees: awake, in the shadow of the living light
entries.digest: Now past seventy, she answered that she had seen the vision in her soul since infancy. She saw it not in sleep, dream or ecstasy, nor with bodily eyes and ears, but awake and alert, by day and night. The light she always saw she called the shadow of the living light; within it she sometimes saw a brighter light, the living light itself, and then all sadness left her.
entries.quote: neither in sleep, nor in dream, nor in madness
entries.source_note: Hildegard to Guibert (CCCM 91A ep. 103r); description per Atherton; English phrase from Singer's 1917 translation as quoted by Foxhall 2014.

entries.headline: The questioner moves in as secretary
entries.digest: After Volmar and Gottfried had died, Guibert came to the Rupertsberg and served as her secretary and provost. He polished her Latin and gathered material for a life of her that he never finished; scholars believe his hand lies behind some of the revised letters.
entries.source_note: Atherton chronology (1177); Hildegard Society FAQ (provost 1177–81); Van Engen 2018 on Guibert's revisions.

entries.headline: Death on the Rupertsberg
entries.digest: Hildegard died aged about eighty-one. The Vita reports that at dusk two bright streams of light appeared in the sky over the room where she lay, forming a cross. This is the biographer's report of a miracle, not a witness's dated note.
entries.source_note: Vita III; date 17 September 1179 is standard.

entries.headline: Finishing the life from her own words
entries.digest: Commissioned after her death, Theoderich completed the Vita by joining Gottfried's book to long passages in her own voice about her visions, her illnesses and the Rupertsberg. Most of what later readers know of her inner life in the 1140s comes through his selection.
entries.source_note: Vita prologues; Wikipedia summary (Theoderic used Gottfried's Libellus and Guibert's materials).

entries.headline: First proposing migraine
entries.digest: Singer presented his reading of Hildegard to the Historical Section of the Royal Society of Medicine, having shared it privately with Arnold Klebs that summer. Looking at the pictures of stars, flames and spreading circles of light, he argued that they matched the visual disturbances of migraine.
entries.source_note: Foxhall 2014, Medical History 58(3).

entries.headline: Scintillating scotoma, in print
entries.digest: In 'The Scientific Views and Visions of Saint Hildegard' Singer closed a long study of her science with a short medical reading. He argued that a physician or migraine sufferer would recognise scintillating scotoma in her descriptions and pictures, while still treating her religious meaning as her own. Foxhall shows how his suggestion became a settled-sounding diagnosis, repeated by Oliver Sacks in 1970.
entries.source_note: Singer, Studies in the History and Method of Science (Oxford 1917); as analysed in Foxhall 2014.

convergences.label: The first outside check: Disibodenberg writes to Clairvaux
convergences.note: She writes at length, in fear, about a secret she has kept; he answers in a few lines. Her letter seeks a verdict, his avoids one, praising grace while declining to teach her.

convergences.label: Winter at Trier: the book goes public
convergences.note: The decisive scene has no eyewitness record: the pope's reading is told by Gottfried decades later, the papal voice survives only in her edited archive, and Hildegard herself was not at Trier. The most important moment is the least documented.

convergences.label: After approval, the questions arrive
convergences.note: A Paris master wants a ruling on a school question; a neighbouring superior wants to know why the nuns wear crowns. Both treat her as newly public property, one as an oracle, one as an anomaly.

convergences.label: The move to the Rupertsberg
convergences.note: Her dictated memoir tells of illness as a sign; the biographer turns Kuno's consent into a conversion; Kuno himself is silent. The same events serve as vision, miracle and property dispute.

convergences.label: Scivias done, Richardis gone
convergences.note: In the year the book was finished, its witness left. Hildegard writes in grief and anger to mother, brother, archbishop and pope; the pope hands it back to Mainz; Richardis herself says nothing that survives.

convergences.label: A death that ends the quarrel
convergences.note: Hartwig's letter is both news and apology; Hildegard's reply converts loss into praise. The only account of Richardis's wish to return comes from the brother who had sent her away.

convergences.label: One visionary writes to another
convergences.note: Elisabeth's angel spoke forecasts that failed; Hildegard, already approved, warns that the prophet is only a trumpet. The older woman's earlier caution in going public becomes advice.

convergences.label: How does she see? Questions, answers, and a life being written
convergences.note: While Gottfried was composing the official life, an outsider asked directly how the visions came. Her answer, waking and alert, is the source Singer would later read through a medical lens.

convergences.label: The same words, read eight centuries later
convergences.note: She insisted the light came neither in sleep nor dream nor madness; Singer accepted that she was awake and read it as a neurological event. Both agree on the wakefulness; they disagree on what it means.

ties.note: Her teacher, confessor and scribe from 1141 until his death in 1173; the 'faithful man' of the Scivias preface.
Exchanged letters in 1146–47; the Vita says Bernard spoke for her at Trier.
Eugenius had been Bernard's monk at Clairvaux and was guided by him in many affairs.
Her superior, who resisted the move to the Rupertsberg and whom she later blamed in the Richardis affair.
Nun of her community and witness to the writing of Scivias; their separation in 1151 drew Hildegard's most emotional letters.
Brother and sister; Bassum lay in Hartwig's diocese.
She appealed to him to return his sister; he later admitted fault.
Elisabeth wrote for consolation in 1155; Hildegard replied with the trumpet image. Their communities were a day's journey apart.
Tengswich questioned her community's customs; Hildegard defended them.
Exchanged letters c. 1148–50 on a disputed theological question.
Correspondent from 1175, her secretary at the Rupertsberg from 1177.
Theoderich completed the Vita that Gottfried left unfinished at his death in 1176.
Singer studied her manuscripts and the Guibert letter to build his 1913–17 migraine reading.

threads_out.note: Hildegard insisted to Guibert that her visions came neither in sleep nor in dreams, setting her claim apart from the dream-interpretation books and dream visions that circulated in the medieval West. Her case shows a visionary drawing the line between dreaming and seeing.

Her account of seeing while fully awake, and Singer's 1917 neurological reading of the same words, are an early case of a waking insight later explained as a brain event; Oliver Sacks took up Singer's diagnosis in Migraine (1970).

The Riesenkodex, which holds Scivias, the letters and the Vita, stayed at the Rupertsberg until the seventeenth century, when the nuns carried it away during the Thirty Years' War; it later passed to Eibingen and then to Wiesbaden.

The illuminated Rupertsberg Scivias was evacuated to Dresden for safekeeping in 1945 and has been lost ever since; its pictures survive only in a 1920s hand-painted facsimile and a black-and-white microfilm.
